lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand the role of neurotransmitters at synapses

primer.text: You already know neurones carry electrical impulses at high speed. This note covers the one place that story has a gap — literally: neurones never touch, and the tiny space between them is bridged by chemicals called neurotransmitters. Learn the handover sequence, because reflex-arc questions routinely test the synapse step.

modules.title: Crossing the synaptic gap
modules.opening: Neurones never quite touch. Between them sits a synapse — a microscopic gap — and that gap is where chemistry takes over: an arriving impulse makes the first neurone release neurotransmitters, which diffuse across and spark a fresh impulse in the next cell.
keyPoints: Neurones are separated by tiny gaps called synapses.
An arriving electrical impulse triggers neurotransmitter release at the end of a neurone.
Neurotransmitters diffuse over the gap and attach to the next neurone.
Binding generates a new impulse, relaying the message between the separate cells.

low.restatement: Impulse arrives, chemicals cross the gap, next neurone fires — the synapse relays signals between separate cells.
low.analogy: A synapse is a river between islands: the message boards a ferry (the neurotransmitter) to cross.
low.examPointer: Remember both halves: chemical crossing, then a NEW electrical impulse — the impulse itself never jumps.

medium.restatement: Because neurones are not directly connected, transmission needs a chemical bridge: arriving impulses trigger neurotransmitter release, diffusion crosses the gap, and binding regenerates the electrical signal.
medium.analogy: Think of a relay race where the baton is thrown across a short gap rather than handed over.
medium.examPointer: Questions ask what neurotransmitters do — 'diffuse across the synapse and bind' earns the marks; 'travel along the neurone' does not.

glossary.definition: The tiny gap between two neurones across which signals are carried chemically.
A chemical messenger released at a synapse that diffuses across and binds to the next neurone, generating a new impulse.
The spreading of molecules from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, here across the synaptic gap.
